reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: The reader will learn to pick among advice, nudge, tax and mandate for a technical decision and to judge governance by how long decisions wait.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Key points: teams decide by default after advice and record it; stronger instruments (nudge, tax) follow the cost of divergence; mandates are the costliest and rarest, kept on a short reasoned list.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: The chapter addresses two failure patterns: the Review Bottleneck (an approving board) and the Consensus Stall (advice mistaken for agreement).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Corvane's architecture forum approved nearly everything after a 23-day median wait, yet the technology landscape diverged anyway, and now three teams want a fourth broker.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) the thesis that a technical decision should be made as close to the work as the cost of divergence allows, with advice-and-record as default, nudge or tax where consistency pays, and mandate only for risk a team cannot carry; (2) the roadmap of the chapter's sections.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: A Forum That Approves and a Landscape Nobody Chose ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: How Corvane's forum was set up: five senior engineers, meeting fortnightly, whose approval was required before any design adding a technology or changing a cross-team interface.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: A Forum That Approves and a Landscape Nobody Chose ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: After a year the rule produced a queue that approved almost everything unchanged while the landscape kept spreading, because the forum judged each design alone and never asked what it cost other teams.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: A Forum That Approves and a Landscape Nobody Chose ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Three teams request a new broker to replay schedule-change events; the forum's next slot is five weeks off, its members know less than the requesters, and nobody represents the two teams on the oldest broker.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why a Central Board Is the Wrong Default ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The strongest case for the architecture-board model: some choices should be made once company-wide, and Ross, Weill and Robertson list compliance and exception processes to hold projects to standards.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why a Central Board Is the Wrong Default ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The first fault of an approving board is that it is a queue that grows with the company while the board stays the same size, which is the Review Bottleneck and consumes verification capacity.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why a Central Board Is the Wrong Default ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) the second fault is information, since the board knows far less about the problem than the team does; (2) the resulting principle: move decisions to where the information is and keep central only what has a high cost of divergence, a cost made up of relearning, repeated fixes, operating burden and risk.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: The Advice Process and the Decision Record ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The advice process (Harmel-Law): anyone may make an architectural decision provided they first consult those affected and those with expertise; advice must be sought and recorded but need not be followed, and the decider stays accountable.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: The Advice Process and the Decision Record ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Advice and decision are written in a short decision record (ADR) in Nygard's format, whose five parts plus two additions are tabulated.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: The Advice Process and the Decision Record ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: A record becomes a governance instrument only if others can find it in one searchable place and a later record can supersede it without the old one being edited or erased.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: The Advice Process and the Decision Record ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: To give teams somewhere to ask for advice, the author recommends a weekly, open advisory forum that has no power to approve.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: The Advice Process and the Decision Record ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The pattern is measured by the days from a team's question to its recorded decision, kept honest by the share of records that include outside advice.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Advice cannot stop a team making a choice that is good for it but costly for others, so governance needs three stronger influences from Grounded Architecture: nudges, taxes and mandates.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A nudge makes the preferred choice the easy one without forbidding anything; in engineering it is the default embodied in a paved path that teams may leave.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: A tax leaves the choice with the team but makes it bear the cost it imposes on others, either in money (cloud chargeback) or, as the author extends it, in operating work for a technology nobody else runs.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: A mandate says what teams must or must not do, is reserved for compliance, security and strategic constraints, and works best as an automatically checked guardrail.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: A table compares the four instruments by who decides, how each acts and what each costs the organization.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Instruments Above Advice: Nudge, Tax and Mandate ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: A mandate is the costliest instrument because it needs enforcement and breeds exception requests, overrides the team's knowledge and hides evidence of quality, so mandates should be a last resort kept on one short written list with reasons and owners.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Three ordered questions choose the instrument: is there risk the team cannot carry, does the cost fall on others, and is there (or should there be) a paved path; a figure maps the answers, and a team whose cost stays internal simply has nobody it must consult.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A table runs four example decisions through the three questions to show the range of outcomes.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Start with the weakest instrument that could work and raise it only on evidence: low adoption of a path first questions the path, then a tax, and a mandate only on demonstrated harm; an instrument can also be lowered.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The right mix of instruments changes with company size, shown in a table of the author's expected mix at Corvane's five sizes (not what Corvane actually did).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) the users of the instruments are the teams that choose and the teams that live with the result; (2) the instruments are working when teams stay on paved paths by choice, the mandate list stays short and decisions do not wait.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Who Carries Governance: Architects as Connectors ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The instruments do not run themselves: advice, paved paths and the mandate list all depend on staff-plus engineers and architects.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Who Carries Governance: Architects as Connectors ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Governance asks these people to connect, riding Hohpe's elevator between strategy and code as 'super glue', so their main product is a better decision made by someone else.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Who Carries Governance: Architects as Connectors ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) their four governance jobs are giving early advice, turning repeated advice into paths or guardrails, keeping the mandate list short, and feeding team learning back into the strategy; (2) they should be judged by the decisions they improved and the repeated advice they made unnecessary.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Anti-Patterns: The Gate, the Stall and the Growing Rulebook ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The Review Bottleneck returns whenever teams wait for a forum before acting, recognisable by finished designs being presented, near-universal approval and work stopping until the hearing.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Anti-Patterns: The Gate, the Stall and the Growing Rulebook ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The Consensus Stall appears when a board is removed without saying who decides and teams wait for every adviser to agree; the fix is that advice is heard and recorded, then the team decides and names dissenters.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Anti-Patterns: The Gate, the Stall and the Growing Rulebook ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Mandate lists grow after every incident and never shrink until teams treat all rules as negotiable; the remedy is a short list where each mandate has a reason and owner and is removed when the reason goes.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane's New Broker ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) Corvane changed its forum from approving to advising, meeting weekly and deciding nothing; (2) Vance and Haddad then sorted the landscape's open questions by cost of divergence (table).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane's New Broker ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The three teams wrote one record, consulted the affected teams and two experts, and the advice both confirmed the need and changed the proposal so the new broker replaces the oldest instead of becoming a fourth.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane's New Broker ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The record settled who pays and what is planned: the three teams operate the new broker as a tax, the platform team owns the migration and switch-off date, and Vance adds a temporary mandate against any further broker until then.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: Corvane's New Broker ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The result: the decision was recorded in twelve days and the median later fell to six, at the stated cost of running four brokers until the switch-off.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What AI Changes Here ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) the book's convention that AI claims carry a Proven, Emerging or Speculative label, and the question of what happens to records, guardrails and boards when agents write code; (2) the Emerging claim that teams feed decision records and paved-path templates to coding agents so decisions and guardrails reach agent-written code, based on the author's observation only.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What AI Changes Here ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Speculative claim: if agents multiply changes, human boards fall further behind and unautomated mandates go unenforced; Corvane's 2027-28 sprawl of agents is sorted by the same three questions (data egress a guardrailed mandate, agent choice a nudge).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: What the sources agree on: some choices are company-wide business decisions, defaults are powerful choice-preserving nudges, advice is not consensus and the decider stays accountable, and records are short and superseded, not erased.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: What depends on context: which choices deserve consistency, where the mandate line falls, and whether a forum is needed at a given size.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The author's own contributions: the single scale of force ordered by cost of divergence, the operating-work tax, raising instruments only on evidence, and measuring governance by decision wait time.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checklist ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The four instruments form one scale read by how far a choice's cost travels, with the record keeping it visible and reversible; eight checks follow for auditing one's own approvals, mandates, wait times, records, paved paths and advisers.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checklist ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Two ideas: (1) a recap that Corvane's forum failed as a queue and the broker was settled by advice, tax and a recorded plan, leaving leaders one number to watch, the decision wait; (2) the hand-off: a paved path must be built and chosen like a product, which the next chapter on platforms takes up.

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 41 aligned units match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01 to p38 with p12b, p16b, p20b; p21 before p20b as the spec now orders them). The three opening callouts match no spec paragraph by house format. The synthesis sits in Checklist ¶1 with the eight checks and the so-what in the closing paragraph, inside the conclusion by house format.

Seven units were marked two_ideas (Introduction ¶2, Why a Central Board ¶3, Choosing the Instrument ¶5, Who Carries Governance ¶3, Worked Example ¶1, What AI Changes Here ¶1, Checklist ¶2). In each, both ideas are in the spec paragraph's controlling idea (p02 thesis and route; p08 information fault and the principle; p20b users and measures; p24 four jobs and how they are judged; p28 the changed rule and the sorted landscape; p38 the Corvane explanation and the hand-off), or the extra is the label announcement that the book's convention puts first in the AI section (p32).

Every unit supports the supporting claim its section declares (S1 scene and board, S2 advice and record, S3 instruments, S4 choosing, S5 roles, S1/S3 anti-patterns, S2/S4 worked example, S3/S4 AI). No unit is off the thesis.

Every quotation is followed by what it shows (Ross, Weill and Robertson; Hohpe twice; Harmel-Law three times; Nygard; Thaler and Sunstein; Grounded Architecture four times), each of the six tables is introduced with what to read in it and is used by the next unit, and Figure 1 has a lead-in and a caption. Not failed, noted: two details of spec evidence are absent from the draft without loss to what the evidence shows (p04 'teams start work before approval or cut designs to stay under the rule'; p06 the IT engagement model), and p27's remedy says a mandate whose reason has gone is removed where the spec says the list is reviewed on a rhythm. Figure 1's nudge-or-tax fork differs from the figure the spec describes; that is recorded under flow_is_followable.

Every declared transition is expressed at its boundary, e.g. 'Here is the situation in full' (elaboration), 'A year of that rule produced a queue' (cause_effect), 'The need is real, and the mechanism is where the model goes wrong' (contrast), 'The second fault is information' (additional_support), 'A record is written by one team, and the advice in it has to come from somewhere' (sequence), 'Advice has a limit' (contrast), 'With all three defined' (conclusion_summary), 'An instrument, once chosen, is not fixed' (elaboration), 'None of these instruments runs by itself' (cause_effect), 'The opposite failure appears' (contrast), 'The model above was described for people who write code' (additional_support, after the label sentence the convention requires). Two boundaries are weak but readable: p15→p16 has no connective and carries the contrast by content ('leaves the choice with the team' against 'must or must not do'), and p29→p30 opens with 'also', which reads as addition where cause_effect is declared, the causal step being the last sentence of p29 ('So the record proposed').

Both flow readers describe the organising principle as problem, diagnosis, remedy by rising force, operation, application, which agrees with the declared problem_solution with small_to_large and prerequisite_order. Neither marks any section's position unclear and neither wants any section moved. Local lost-thread points are separate failed results; two of them are corroborated.

Every does_not_know term is given at or before first use in the body: cost of divergence (KEY POINTS, Introduction ¶2, again in Why a Central Board ¶3), advice process (p09), decision record/ADR (p10), nudge and paved path (p14), tax (p15), mandate and guardrail (p16), staff-plus roles (p22, with the link to chapter 21); 'architecture governance' is given as who decides technical direction and with how much force; message broker is glossed in Introduction ¶1. Both flow readers confirm these. Not failed: reader 1 (3.10, b, slight) paused at 'the delivery path', which falls under the audience's already_knows (deployment); reader 2 (3.8, b) paused at 'the term from the lead', an editor's word, with the definition repeated in the same sentence.
The introduction opens on a concrete puzzling case and states the thesis outright; the cold reader of the introduction found none of the weak patterns.
The conclusion sorts what holds by how settled it is, adds a synthesis and a course of action and returns to the opening case; it does not merely restate the thesis and opens no new subtopic.

Synthesis is present ('The four instruments are one scale with one rule for reading it. The further the cost of a choice travels from the team that makes it, the more force the organization may use. The record is what keeps every point on the scale visible and reversible.') and so is the so-what ('A leader who replaces most approvals with advice and records, and keeps a short written list of mandates, can then watch one number: how long a decision waits.'). The takeaway is the eight-item checklist.

The closing paragraph returns to the forum and the broker and answers both halves of the opening puzzle: 'Corvane's forum was slow because it was a queue, and its landscape diverged because approving one design at a time never asked what a choice cost the other teams. The new broker was adopted by decision of the three teams that needed it, after advice, with a tax and a migration plan in the record.'

The cold reader of the introduction predicted nine parts in the order of the roadmap and of the sections, the thesis, the Corvane case as main evidence and a plain first-person tone. It noted only that the decision-wait measure promised in the first callout is not placed by the roadmap.

The cold reader assigned (1) advice at most, strictly none: cost inside the team, cheap to change; (2) mandate checked as a guardrail: legal exposure no team can carry; (3) tax reached through the advice process and a decision record: the team operates what it alone adopted; (4) nudge by the paved path, stepping to a tax and to a mandate only on evidence of harm. All four agree with the expected answer; three were reached by applying the three questions to cases the chapter does not contain.

Who Carries Governance ¶1 says why governance relies on the roles (advice needs someone who knows several teams' systems, a paved path someone who notices repeated advice, a mandate list an owner), names them ('This book calls them the staff-plus roles and defines them in [[staff-plus-and-architects]]') and ¶3 gives their four jobs in governance.

Each borrowed concept names its source and the concept (Enterprise Architecture as Strategy; The Software Architect Elevator; Nudge; Grounded Architecture, named each time; Harmel-Law's article; Nygard's post). The author's own rules and extensions are marked ('My extension, which *Grounded Architecture* does not make', 'three reasons that are my own argument', 'I add one discipline', 'My rule is', 'The placement is my synthesis', 'My addition', 'I report it from experience'), and the conclusion separates Established, Depends on context and The author's synthesis. The conclusion now says 'a default is a powerful nudge', which is what the source says.

Each pattern names its users and an outcome measure: the advice process and record (the deciding team and the teams affected; days from question to recorded decision, with the share of records listing outside advice), the three instruments (the teams that choose and the teams that live with the result; teams on paved paths by choice, a short mandate list, no waiting decision), and the staff-plus roles (teams and executives; decisions improved, visible in records naming their advice, and repeated advice made unnecessary).

results.draft_locus: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶1 (Figure 1)
results.quote: Q2 -->|"no"| A["The team decides: nobody else is affected, so nobody must be consulted"]
results.finding: The lead and the KEY POINTS say that by default the team decides after advice 'and records the decision'. In Figure 1 a decision record appears only on the 'yes' branch ('Advice process and a decision record'), and the first row of the four-decision table gives the instrument as 'None, or advice if the team asks'. The sentence before the figure ('Its second branch does not suspend the default') settles the advice half and not the record half. Both readers were left unsure whether a team whose choice affects nobody still writes a record; the draft never says. One sentence beside the figure settles it.

results.draft_locus: Choosing the Instrument by the Cost of Divergence ¶1 (Figure 1) against ¶3
results.quote: Q3 -->|"no"| T["Tax: the team pays what its choice costs others"]
results.finding: Figure 1 makes nudge and tax alternatives decided by whether a paved path exists (yes: nudge; no: tax), and the caption says force follows how far the cost travels. Two paragraphs later the tax is a step above the nudge ('If teams still leave a good path and the others pay for it, the next step up is a tax'), and the instruments were defined 'from the least force to the most'. Both readers had to go back to the figure and supply the assumption that the figure gives the starting instrument and the later paragraph the escalation; the draft does not say so. The spec's figure (p18 evidence) describes the outcomes as cumulative (advice and record, plus a nudge where a path exists, plus a tax on the divergent choice), and its fourth example row has 'nudge by paved path, tax on leaving it'; the draft's either-or fork and its nudge-only row depart from both. Round 1 failed the opposite wording (a tax inside the nudge box), so the revision should state the relation of the two once and not only redraw the fork.

results.quote: Its second branch does not suspend the default.
results.finding: The sentence and the one after it comment on the figure before the reader has seen it; 'second branch' is not a label in the figure, and the sentence answers an objection the reader has not yet formed. Both readers read on to the figure and came back, and both suggest moving the two sentences after Figure 1. Reader 1 (3.1) rated it (a), reader 2 (3.5) rated it (b), so it is not corroborated under this book's rule.

results.quote: Dario Vance set it, as a temporary mandate with its reason and its end written down.
results.finding: Reader 2 (3.3, a): the reason is said to be written down and is not given. By the three questions a broker choice is a cost on others (advice and a tax), and by the escalation rule a mandate needs incidents or measured cost, so the reader had to supply that running four brokers is the measured cost. The same reader could not tell who decided that the two teams on the oldest broker must migrate ('The three teams decided the adoption'). One reader only.
